title: A systematic review of AI in second language acquisition using the expanded SAMR model (2015–2024)
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI applications in second language acquisition (SLA) primarily enhance existing language-learning tasks or truly transform them. To answer this, the authors systematically reviewed empirical journal articles on AI in SLA published between 2015 and 2024, using the expanded SAMR model to classify each study according to whether technology use left the product and process unchanged, redesigned one of them, or redesigned both.

The review screened Web of Science and Scopus and included 281 studies after full-text assessment. Because this was a review rather than a single classroom intervention, it did not focus on one learner cohort or one instructional setting; instead, it synthesized studies spanning multiple language skills, tools, and contexts. The paper also coded whether studies used generative AI and examined how SAMR levels varied by skill area and year.

The main conclusion is that most AI-in-SLA work still sits at the augmentation level, meaning AI mainly speeds up feedback or makes existing routines more efficient. About 35% of studies reached modification or redefinition, with GenAI appearing more often in later years and especially in transformation-level designs, but not serving as a guarantee of transformation. Writing and speaking dominated the corpus and mostly remained enhancement-oriented, while reading, listening, and vocabulary more often reached higher levels of redesign. The review ends by proposing a GenAI-driven three-stage framework for pre-class, in-class, and post-class use, and argues that deeper transformation requires pedagogical redesign, not just better tools.

identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used for text generation, dialogic support, and feedback in educational settings.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of AI in second language acquisition; it codes empirical studies across SAMR levels and discusses GenAI as an enabler of transformation in literacy-related language tasks, without focusing on a single named product.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with transparent search, screening, and coding procedures, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than reporting a single causal effect estimate. The evidence is observational/descriptive, so it supports mapping and synthesis more than causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests GenAI can enable transformation in some literacy-related designs, but the reported statistical test found no significant overall association between GenAI use and higher SAMR levels. With no effect size and mixed direction, the impact is plausible but unclear.
